doc.title: Albert Murray interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 24, 1997

title: Swing in the depression; people live as human beings, not activists
summary: At the height of the depression came the swing era with affirmative music. Murray says people are concerned with being human rather than ideology.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: seeking your fortune, going to seek your fortune. In America it might mean dollars and cents but in mythology it doesn’t mean dollars and cents. It means your future — your good fortune or whatever was going to befall you, your destiny. You see what I mean? Whereas in America, in some instances, some American writers, it’s all materialistic. Like they can’t understand why those people could be having so much fun and they don’t have the money. They [inaudible] that the people with the fun are not having the money are not having that. They’re worried about the money you see? So they will have these people jumping out of windows because the stock market crashed, or things like that. They responded to it but they responded with affirmative music, with the emphasis on having a good time. I mean that’s the thing. At the height of the depression it was the swing era. That’s where they came in you see? So to get it confused with commiseration and stuff like that, is just to miss what it’s about, and it’s part of the confusion that comes out of what we call racism in America. Look at somebody and decide what they’re about. And you decide what you think you are and then you say they’re not this so they are that you see? And these people are only concerned with being human.

I think the problem is that many people, from the context that I come from, just sort of do what is expected of them. They’re expected to be all activists, involved with this, as if that’s what they live for. And I haven’t found that to be so. I find people are very serious about social issues and things like that. I don’t find that’s what they spend most of their time doing. They end up doing, if they have a family, they try to do what you do as a member of a family, the father or mother of a family, to do what you can do by your children. And if you don’t, they might be going out just having a good time and neglecting their children, but they’re not out there dealing with social problems and addressing themselves to that. They don’t live in terms of that. They live in terms of being human beings and they do what they’re going to do. And they decide they’re going to get this out of life, or they’re going to get that out of life, and they decide maybe it’ll add up to a form of hedonism, or it might add up to something else where a person might say well life is rough but it’s just a sojourn anyway and we get ourselves ready for the afterlife. How is that different from what most of the people in Europe were doing during the middle ages? If you were a soldier, you used to build cathedrals and all. And we look at what they were eating, and where they were sleeping and all, and contrast that with the pride they took in the cathedral that they lived near, you see? If we keep looking at how human beings act, I mean and away from some ideological approach to human motives, you come nearer to understanding what their art form really expresses.
